viNames.name: cá ba đuôi mắt lồi đen

origin.fact: Black moors are thought to come from China in the 1400s. They were traded in Japan in the 1500s and reached the USA in the 1800s.
The same page says the telescope-eye trait itself was first bred in China in the early 1700s, where it was called 'dragon eyes'. In Japan the fish became the Demekin.
Chinese records mention twin-tailed goldfish in the 16th century, so Moors probably appeared around then. They descend from the telescope-eyed line, which came from the twin-tailed Wakin.
A Vietnamese newspaper says Chinese breeders developed the dragon-eye goldfish in the 17th century. Its Chinese name is 出目金.
In 1941, the Moscow aquarist P. Andrianov bred a black telescope with orange-red eyes.
The name 'Moor' refers to the Black Muslim people of Al-Andalus. 'Blackamoor' is an archaic form.

looks.fact: A deep, round body with long flowing double fins and telescope eyes that stick out to the sides.
The best fish have a deep, velvety blue-black colour that reaches the fins and belly.
Top-quality moors look velvety, without metallic shine, but can lose this look with age.
The eyes should point outward and slightly forward, match in size and shape, and be large for the head. Eye shapes can be conical, ringed or round like a balloon.
Body depth should be at least about 65% of body length. The tail should be even and divided, without curled edges.
UK standards ask for a veil tail at least 75% of body length with no fork. The American Goldfish Association accepts both veil and forked tails.
Young fish look like bronze fantails with flat eyes. The black colour and bulging eyes develop with age.
The black comes from extra melanin. Fry are grey at first, and black usually shows from about 5–6 weeks old.
A Vietnamese newspaper describes a short, thick body, sometimes with a rounded hump at the shoulder. It calls Black Moor the most common dragon-eye goldfish.

lines.fact: Panda telescope (panda moor): black and white. Its colours may change to orange-white or fade to all white.
Telescopes also come in white, red, orange and yellow. The black form is the most popular.
Butterfly-tail telescopes are listed as a related breed.

keeping.fact: Allow about 70 L for one fish plus about 45 L for each extra goldfish. Use gentle filtration that turns the water over about 4 times an hour.
A Vietnamese guide gives 75–95 L as the tank size.
Avoid sharp decorations and clutter, because the eyes are easily punctured and a damaged eye does not refill.
Do not keep with normal-eyed goldfish, which get to the food first. Bubble-eyes and celestials, which also see poorly, are suitable tankmates.
Feed adults about 1–2% of body weight a day in several small meals. Gel foods, vegetables and live or frozen foods such as daphnia and bloodworms are good choices.
Sinking food is better than floating food, because the fish have trouble finding food at the surface.
Some keepers advise not keeping moors too warm, because warmth may speed up colour change.
Black moors are hardy and tolerate a wide range of temperatures.

breeding.fact: Black moors breed like other goldfish. Use several males per female, because the telescope eyes make it hard for males to find the female.
Males in breeding condition show white tubercles on the gill covers and pectoral fins.
Black telescopes do not always breed true. They can produce normal-eyed black young, which are usually culled.
A Vietnamese source says the fish mature and can breed at about 6–7 months.
A Vietnamese guide recommends broodstock about 1–2 years old.

health.fact: Poor eyesight makes them slow at getting food and prone to eye injuries and infections.
Swim bladder disorder, often caused by a poor diet in older fish, is the main killer of adults.
They are no more prone to disease than other fancy goldfish and handle cold better than most.
A fish that has lost an eye may need salt baths and watching at feeding time.

buying.fact: Avoid fish with a bronze tint, which may later turn orange or red. Fish with a white or silvery belly are more likely to stay black.
Choose fish with even, matching eyes, a deep body and an even, divided tail.
Young telescopes can be temporarily black and later fade to orange. A true black moor stays black.
Quarantine new fish and treat them as if they carry parasites. A mild salt bath is useful.
Choose fish with bright colour, a balanced body and no signs of disease.

controversy.fact: The UK Companion Animal Welfare Council report 'Breeding and Welfare in Companion Animals' lists telescope goldfish among bred traits that harm welfare. It says the bulging eyes (up to 2 cm) are vulnerable to injury. Critics said the report relied on hobby books rather than new research.
Normal-eyed young from black telescope spawns are often culled.
